related.why: The same look, feel, move structure
Neck pain that mimics shoulder pain

brief.scenario: Mr Gareth Evans, 55, a plasterer, has had right shoulder pain for four months. It is worse when he reaches overhead and when he lies on that side.
brief.task: Examine his right shoulder. You will be stopped at 6 minutes to present your findings and answer questions.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Look from behind, feel, move actively then passively, test each cuff muscle, then the neck.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Forgetting passive external rotation, the one movement that picks up frozen shoulder.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Could you take your top off so I can see both shoulders?"

grid.label: Preparation
grid.fail: Starts moving the arm without asking about pain.
grid.pass: Introduces, confirms identity, gains consent, asks about pain, cleans hands, exposes both shoulders.
grid.high: Asks which movements hurt before starting, and compares with the left side at each step.

grid.label: Look
grid.fail: Inspects from the front only, or through clothing.
grid.pass: Front, side and back: deltoid, supraspinatus and infraspinatus wasting, scars, asymmetry, winging.
grid.high: Explains that supraspinatus or infraspinatus wasting suggests a chronic cuff tear or suprascapular nerve lesion.

grid.label: Feel
grid.pass: Sternoclavicular joint, clavicle, acromioclavicular joint, acromion, greater tuberosity, bicipital groove.
grid.high: Uses ACJ tenderness to separate ACJ arthritis from subacromial pain.

grid.label: Movement
grid.borderline: Tests passive movement but not external rotation with the arm by the side.
grid.pass: Active, then passive: flexion, abduction, external and internal rotation; identifies a painful arc.
grid.high: Tests passive external rotation with the arm by the side: disproportionate loss suggests frozen shoulder; full passive range points to the cuff.

grid.label: Rotator cuff
grid.fail: Tests 'strength' globally without isolating each muscle.
grid.pass: Jobe's (empty can) for supraspinatus, resisted external rotation for infraspinatus, lift-off or belly-press for subscapularis.
grid.high: Adds an external rotation lag sign, and explains that pain with normal strength suggests tendinopathy while weakness suggests a tear.

grid.label: Impingement tests and the neck
grid.pass: Neer's and Hawkins–Kennedy; examines the cervical spine and distal neurovascular status.
grid.high: Explains that tests are read in combination, not singly, and that cervical radiculopathy can mimic shoulder pain.

grid.label: Presentation at the signal
grid.pass: Summarises the positive findings and gives a most likely diagnosis.
grid.high: Leads with the key findings, states the important negatives (full passive range, cuff strength, normal neck), and commits.

grid.label: Management
grid.fail: Lists him for decompression at the first visit.
grid.pass: Clinical diagnosis; analgesia and physiotherapy first; X-ray if trauma, red flags, severe pain or stiffness, or persisting symptoms.
grid.high: One subacromial steroid injection if not improving by 6–8 weeks; secondary care by 12 weeks; surgery considered after six months.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [Starts lifting the arm through his shirt without asking about pain.]

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Lift your arm up… and out to the side. [No passive movement.]

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Push against me with both arms. They feel strong.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: He has shoulder pain when he lifts his arm.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Put him on the list for a subacromial decompression.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel. Can I confirm your name and date of birth? I'd like to examine your right shoulder. Is it painful now? Could you take your top off? [Consent; cleans hands.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Inspects from front, side and behind for wasting, scars and winging.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Palpates SCJ, clavicle, ACJ, acromion, greater tuberosity and bicipital groove.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Raise your arm forwards… and out to the side. [Painful arc.] Now let me move it. [Passive range.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Arms out, thumbs down, push up against me. [Jobe's.] Elbows at your side, push out. [Resisted external rotation.] Hand behind your back, lift it away from me. [Lift-off.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Neer's; Hawkins–Kennedy.] Could you look up, down and to each side? [Distal pulses and sensation.] Thank you. [Cleans hands.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Mr Evans has no wasting, tenderness below the acromion, a painful arc in mid-abduction, a full passive range, a painful but strong Jobe's test, and positive Neer's and Hawkins–Kennedy tests. His neck is normal. This is most likely subacromial pain.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: It's a clinical diagnosis. Analgesia and physiotherapy first. I'd X-ray if there's trauma, red flags, severe pain or stiffness, or persisting symptoms, as here after four months.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel. Can I confirm your name and date of birth? I'd like to examine both shoulders. Which movements hurt? Could you take your top off? [Consent; cleans hands.]

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Front, side and behind.] No wasting of supraspinatus or infraspinatus, which would suggest a chronic cuff tear or nerve lesion.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Palpates each structure.] The ACJ isn't tender, so ACJ arthritis is less likely.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Active range; painful arc.] Now I'll move it for you, with your elbow at your side. [Passive external rotation equal to the left.] That makes frozen shoulder unlikely.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Jobe's; resisted external rotation; lift-off; external rotation lag.] It's painful but strong, which fits tendinopathy rather than a tear.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Examines the neck first; then Neer's and Hawkins–Kennedy.] I read these together, not singly. [Distal neurovascular status.] Thank you. [Cleans hands.]

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Right shoulder: a painful arc, tenderness below the acromion, positive Neer's and Hawkins–Kennedy, and a painful but strong Jobe's. Importantly, full passive external rotation, no weakness or lag, and a normal neck. This is subacromial pain without a cuff tear.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Analgesia and physiotherapy. If he isn't improving by 6 to 8 weeks, one subacromial steroid injection can be considered; if not better by 12 weeks, secondary care. Surgery is considered only if non-surgical treatment has failed by six months.

failures.consequence: Misses ACJ arthritis as the source of pain.
Misses cervical radiculopathy presenting as shoulder pain.
Can't separate frozen shoulder (passive loss) from cuff pathology (passive range preserved).

recovery.line: Before I finish, I'd like to check passive external rotation with your elbow at your side.
I'd also like to examine your neck, because neck problems can cause pain in the shoulder.

knowledge.fact: Subacromial pain is a clinical diagnosis; use Hawkins–Kennedy, Neer's, Jobe's and resisted external rotation in combination.
Physiotherapy first; one steroid injection if not improving by 6–8 weeks; secondary care by 12 weeks; surgery considered after six months of failed treatment.
Frozen shoulder: disproportionately severe loss of passive external rotation; strongest association is diabetes.
Frozen shoulder is a clinical diagnosis. Routine X-rays rarely change it, but an X-ray excludes arthritis, a missed posterior dislocation, avascular necrosis or a tumour, which can mimic it.
Sudden loss of active elevation, with or without trauma: suspect an acute cuff tear; urgent referral within 2 weeks.

recall.say: "Now I'll move it for you, with your elbow at your side."
do: Jobe's, external rotation, lift-off; then the neck
recall.trap: Painful arc with lost passive rotation isn't impingement.
recall.finish: Physiotherapy first; surgery only after failed non-surgical care.

sources.supports: Urgent referral (within 2 weeks) for sudden loss of ability to actively raise the arm, with or without trauma: acute cuff tear; same-day referral for suspected infection or unreduced dislocation

partner.opening: Please examine this patient's right shoulder. I'll stop you at 6 minutes.
partner.actorBrief: You are Mr Gareth Evans, 55, a plasterer, right-handed. Four months of pain over the outer upper arm, worse reaching overhead and lying on it. No injury, no neck pain, no pins and needles. You are not diabetic. Wince when the arm passes through the middle of its arc going up.

reveals.finding: No wasting, scars, asymmetry or winging.
Tender just below the anterolateral acromion. ACJ not tender.
Painful arc in mid-abduction; pain eases above it.
Full passive range, including external rotation with the arm by the side, equal to the left.
Jobe's painful but strong. External rotation and lift-off strong. No lag.
Neer's and Hawkins–Kennedy positive. Neck full and painless. Neurovascular status normal.
Say: "Please stop there and present your findings."

push.question: How do you tell frozen shoulder from a cuff problem?
push.expect: Passive external rotation: lost in frozen shoulder, preserved with cuff pathology.

push.question: Does he need an X-ray?
push.expect: Not needed to make the diagnosis; indicated for trauma, red flags, severe pain or stiffness, or persisting symptoms, so reasonable after four months.

push.question: What does a lag sign mean?
push.expect: A large full-thickness cuff tear involving supraspinatus and infraspinatus.

curveballs.prompt: He fell last week and now can't lift his arm.
curveballs.safeAnswer: X-ray to exclude fracture or dislocation, and check axillary nerve function. If the X-ray is normal, suspect an acute cuff tear: urgent referral to the shoulder team within 2 weeks for imaging (usually ultrasound) and consideration of early repair.

curveballs.prompt: Passive external rotation is almost absent.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Likely frozen shoulder, a clinical diagnosis. An X-ray won't confirm it, but I'd use it to exclude arthritis, avascular necrosis, a missed posterior dislocation or a tumour.

curveballs.prompt: The pain runs to his hand, with tingling in the thumb.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Think C6 radiculopathy: examine the neck and do a neurological examination of the arm.
Explain that physiotherapy comes first and that surgery is considered only after non-surgical treatment has failed.
